# A callback can re-enter the function that calls it, through the object it is handed

Status: `open`: the change is crustify `6ad1ea5` on `libgit2-crustify/evolution/callback-reenters-its-caller`, made on
2026-11-14 at the user's direction after the triage of open proposals, awaiting its review.

Goal: Safety, its soundness measure.

## Signal

A rule the how-to skills lack, which a binding had to work out by hand (`evolution` §2).
`binding-symbols`' Function pointers section has a trampoline refuse "a re-entrant call,
which would alias an `FnMut` closure": the hazard it names is the closure's state. It says
nothing of the function that runs the callback, whose own state the callback can reach when
C hands it the object the function is working on. Re-entering that function, or resetting
the object, from the callback is then undefined behaviour in C, reachable from safe Rust.

## Evidence

`wave-194/batch-1/run-1` (`deps/llhttp/llhttp.c`'s `llhttp__internal_execute`, bound as
`ParserMut::parse`). The parser's settings name callbacks C calls with the parser being
parsed, so a Rust handler receives that parser's exclusive handle, from which a safe API
offers `parse` and `reinit`. A nested `llhttp__internal_execute` on the same parser sets
`_span_pos0` into the nested input and moves `_index`; the outer run, resuming after the
callback, then hands a span callback `(state->_span_pos0, p)` across two allocations (a
wild length), and `llparse__match_sequence*` index their blobs with the nested `_index`.
`llhttp__internal_init` from a callback nulls `_span_pos0`, which a span-end state reads
back as its start. The batch refuses both with a panic, through a thread-local register of
the parsers each thread is executing, which the trampolines' barrier turns into the
callback's error (`tests/ub_unsafe/deps/llhttp/llhttp.rs`,
`a_handler_cannot_parse_the_parser_whose_parse_runs_it`,
`a_handler_cannot_initialise_the_parser_whose_parse_runs_it`).

## Destination

The spec: `binding-symbols`, Function pointers, beside the trampoline's re-entry rule; and
`analysis`' Findings, which should list it as something the analysis establishes.

## Change

Not made yet. In `binding-symbols` § Function pointers, after the paragraph on the
trampoline's re-entry refusal:

> A function that calls a callback with an object it is working on lends that object to
> the callback. The analysis establishes which of the object's routines C allows from
> within the callback; a routine it does not, the function itself or one that resets the
> state the function resumes from, is refused there by the binding, on the thread that
> runs the function, since the callback holds an exclusive handle the borrow checker
> cannot tell from any other.

In `analysis` § Findings, under states and transitions: "the calls a callback may make on
the object its caller lends it, and those that would corrupt the caller's state".

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands:

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a function that hands a callback the object it is working on lends it; the analysis establishes which of the object's routines C allows from the callback, and the binding refuses the others there | `libgit2-crustify`, `callback-reenters-its-caller` | crustify `6ad1ea5` | a callback could re-enter or reset the function running it through the object it was handed, C undefined behaviour reachable from safe Rust | a `ub` finding of the `callback-state` pattern where a callback calls a routine of the object its caller lent it | watched |

## Validation

None run: the rule is the one this batch followed; a rerun of the batch under it would
produce the same binding. The batch's two UB tests above, run under ASan+UBSan, Miri (they
stop at the foreign call) and BSan alone, are its evidence that the refusal holds.

---
name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, and where the record of what landed is kept. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson; `evolution-record` holds the record and how evolution itself evolves."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per
proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
  and the index's writer records it;
- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
- otherwise, the run files the proposal.

A lesson is not filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it. A defect in a tool found
while reviewing is a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed code, and is filed with its
reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each lesson is one entry, under a heading that is its id: a short
slug no other lesson of the file has. An entry holds a status, one rule, the evidence the

# Evolution record

The record of what [`evolution`](../SKILL.md) landed, and what evolution learns from it.

## 1. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. A row gives the campaign and proposal the change came
from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence signal
and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change no
proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came from.
A proposal that lands several changes takes a row for each.

A change's row is drafted in its proposal, so that the review reads it. The record's writer
copies the row into the record when the change lands. An evolution branch never edits
`EVOLUTION.md`, so that two changes awaiting review never conflict there, and the record
has one writer per campaign. The record holds every change landed since it began, on
2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the row: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that passed
  it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

A row's signal is looked for at two times, in every campaign:

- when a proposal is indexed, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Proposals section describes:
  a signal that matches a row's recurrence signal marks that row `recurred`; and
- periodically, when the rows still `watched` are read against the findings, failed runs,
  proposals and corrections since the last reading. The campaign sets the period from its
  state, shorter after a change to a check lands or while findings cluster, longer while
  its modules are small: by default, after every fifth module it integrates. The rows are
  always read at each ship point and at an audit's end.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign and reaches `devel`
with it. Rows are appended in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge
of two campaigns' working branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the readings still run and their statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, they do not run.

## 2. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Signals section lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Autonomy section describes.

# Authoring

How Crustify is organized: its skills, its agents and the providers that serve them to an
agent host, and where each kind of text lives. The aim is that every rule is written once,
in the one place its kind belongs, so that changing it changes every agent that follows it,
and no two copies drift apart.

## 1. Layers

Crustify is text in three layers, with one more per run:

| layer | where | voice | holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| skills | `skills/<group>/<name>/SKILL.md` | descriptive, third person | what Crustify's artifacts are and how its work is done: workflows, how-tos, conventions, schemas |
| tool skills | `skills/tools/<tool>/SKILL.md` | descriptive, third person | what each tool is, and how it serves each stage |
| agents | `agents/<agent>.md`, with `agents/common.md`, and the assistant's under `agents/assistant/` | instructive, second person | an agent's identity, inputs, what it owns, its steps and what its role changes in the skill index |
| task messages | `task.md` beside a run's `task.json` | instructive | what one run is given: its inputs, and what it needs beyond its role |

Each artifact's schema, the meaning of its fields, is a skill under `skills/artifacts/`,
and an example of each is given under `templates/`, which the schema cites. The settings,
dashboard and `.gitignore` templates there are what a campaign copies to start. Examples
hold illustrations, not rules.

The layers are plain Markdown, so that any agent reads them as files. A provider, under
`providers/<host>/`, serves them to one agent host in its own format, as
[Providers](#4-providers) describes; the layers name no host.

### 1.1 Skills

A skill describes. It states what an artifact holds, how a decision is made, what a
procedure produces and when each of its steps happens, never what an agent should do, and
never who does a step: which agent owns which step is the agents'. It does not name the
tools that serve it either: a skill reads the same whether or not a tool is installed, so
a statement such as "each unit's lifecycle role is established while planning" belongs in
a skill, and the wavefront command that records it belongs in wavefront's tool skill.

Skills are grouped by the part of the work they describe: `workflows/`, `planning/`,
`rust/`, `verification/`, `operations/`, `artifacts/`, `tools/` and `crustify/`. A skill's
name is unique across the groups, since agents invoke it by name. Two kinds of skill
describe how work is done. A how-to, such as `binding` or `porting`, describes how one item
is handled. A workflow, under `workflows/`, describes how one kind of campaign proceeds
from its settings to its results: `setup`, which every campaign shares, and one per kind of
campaign (`binding-workflow`, `porting-workflow`, `audit-workflow`). A workflow names the
how-tos and the layout rather than restating them.

A skill opens with frontmatter that gives its `name` and its `description`. The
description is all an agent sees of the skill before it reads it, so it says what the skill
covers and before which step it is read. A skill stays under about 4,500 tokens, so that a
host that brings an invoked skill back after compacting an agent's context brings it back
whole; one that outgrows that is split at a section that another step needs on its own.
The parts sit in sub-directories of the skill's own, `skills/<group>/<skill>/<part>/SKILL.md`,
each named `<skill>-<part>`, and the skill's own `SKILL.md` keeps what they share: `binding`
and `porting` keep their boundaries, and their `-types` and `-symbols` parts their routes.

A skill's directory may also hold a script the skill describes, with its tests beside it,
standard library only, so that it runs wherever the skill is read: `usage` holds
`crustify-usage`.

A skill or an agent says what a step does and which program does it, never the program's
command lines, flags or options, which change with the program: the program's own `--help`
and documentation give them, and the text sends its reader there. A command appears only
where its exact form is what must hold, and a procedure of several commands that must run
exactly so is a script beside its skill, documented by its own `--help`.

Every skill's sections are numbered. A reference to a section names it, with or without its
number ("testing-builds' Coverage section", "layout § Lifecycle › Waves"), so that a renumbering
never silently points a reference at another section. A skill links another by its
relative path, with the other's name as the link's text.

### 1.2 Agents

An agent instructs. Its file holds what is specific to it: its place among the agents, its
inputs, its workflow steps, and the guidelines that apply to one step or stage. Where a step
follows a skill, the agent names the skill's section rather than restating it ("as the
`scheduling` skill's Order section describes"); where a step adds to it, the agent states
only the addition.

An agent states what it owns by naming the skill sections it carries out ("you create and
purge every level of the `layout` skill's Lifecycle section"), and adds only what the
skills leave to it: the commands it runs, the judgements it makes, the cases it must not
handle itself.

Every agent's prompt opens with `agents/common.md`: that every commit takes the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives, that a task
message's instructions take precedence over the rest of the prompt, except where a skill or a
role says a task message adds to a check and never relaxes it, and how skills and
tool skills are read. Every agent sees every skill, with its description:
its host lists them, or, for a host that does not, the provider fills the index of every
skill at common's `<!-- SKILL INDEX -->` marker from the skills' names and descriptions, so
that each description is written once.

The agent's own file follows, in three sections, every agent alike:

- `## Role`: who the agent is, its place among the agents, what it owns and what it leaves
  to others;
- `## Workflow`: its steps, each naming the skills it follows. A skill the description
  already sends the agent to before a step needs no mention; a step names a skill where
  only part of it applies to the agent, or where the agent follows it only in some runs;
  and
- `## Inputs`: what its task message names.

An agent's file names no value of one run: an integration branch or a batch id is "the one
your task message names". `{crustify_root}` stands for the path of Crustify's checkout,
which a provider fills.

The assistant has one file for every kind of campaign, `agents/assistant/assistant.md`, with a
`<!-- CAMPAIGN ROLE -->` marker at the end of its Role and a `<!-- CAMPAIGN WORKFLOW -->`
marker as its Workflow, which take the campaign kind's file,
`agents/assistant/translate.md` for a port or wrap campaign or `agents/assistant/audit.md`
for an audit: its `### Campaign` section, what the assistant owns in that kind of campaign,
and, after its `<!-- WORKFLOW -->` marker, its steps.

### 1.3 Tool skills

A tool is one program an agent reaches for: wavefront, ffimap, ffibox. Each has one skill,

campaign, and how the tool's output becomes Crustify's artifacts and decisions. How the

documentation's, which the skill cites by document rather than restating, so that the two
never drift; a fact that documentation lacks is added to it, on a branch of the tool's
repository, not to the skill.

A tool skill opens with what the tool is, which documentation of its own is read in full
before its first use, and what holds in every use of it; one section per stage follows,
each subsection named after the skill section it adds to ("Scheduling › Order"), stating
only what the tool adds there and naming the documents of the tool that stage reads. Its
description names the stages and steps it serves.

An agent reads a tool's skill before the first step of its work that the skill's
description names, as `agents/common.md` says, and no other skill names a tool: the
description alone brings an agent to the tool, so it names every stage and step the tool
serves. A tool is removed by deleting its skill.

## 2. Placement

| text | goes in |
|---|---|
| what an artifact's fields mean | its schema skill under `skills/artifacts/` |
| what an artifact looks like | its example under `templates/` |
| how a kind of work is done, independent of tools | the skill for that work |
| how a kind of campaign proceeds, step by step | its workflow skill under `skills/workflows/`, with the steps every campaign shares in `setup` |
| a convention every agent follows | `conventions` |
| what one agent does, in which steps, and which steps it owns | that agent's file under `agents/` |
| what every agent holds | `agents/common.md` |
| what the assistant does in one kind of campaign | `agents/assistant/<kind>.md` |
| what a tool is, and how it serves each stage | its tool skill |
| how one host is served the layers | its provider under `providers/<host>/` |
| what one run needs beyond its role | its task message, `task.md` |
| what Crustify is for, which every change is judged against | `GOALS.md`, at Crustify's root |
| how Crustify repairs and improves itself | [`evolution`](../evolution/SKILL.md) |
| which changes landed, and whether each held | `EVOLUTION.md`, at Crustify's root |
| a rule that holds for one target alone | that campaign's `crustify/LESSONS.md` |

A rule that two agents share goes in a skill both read, not in both agents. A rule that
names a tool goes in the tool's skill. A change to a rule is made where the rule lives;
text that restates it elsewhere is removed rather than kept in step.

## 3. Runs

A stage's agent runs with its file as its system prompt and its task as its first message:
the task message names what its `## Inputs` section lists and the instructions its run
needs beyond its role, if any. Its file is the same for every run of the stage, so that runs at once share their
whole system prompt in the provider's cache. The assistant runs the same way, as the main
agent of a session in a campaign's repository, with its file and its campaign kind's as
its system prompt.

## 4. Providers

A provider serves the layers to one agent host, in that host's format, and holds nothing
the layers do not: every file it carries is generated from them, wires them in, or carries
what its host needs of its own.

The generic provider, `providers/generic/`, composes each agent's prompt for any host:
`compose.py <agent> [<kind>]` prints `agents/common.md`, with the skill index filled, and
the agent's file, the assistant's with its campaign kind's. A host without a provider of
its own takes that prompt as its agent's instructions, and reads each skill's `SKILL.md`
by its path. The other providers compose through it.

The Claude Code provider, `providers/claude/`, makes Crustify's checkout a plugin, whose
manifest is `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`:

- the skills, by their group directories and the directory of each part of a split skill,
  which the manifest lists on its own since Claude Code scans a listed directory one level
  deep, invoked as `crustify:<name>`;
- `agents/`, one plugin agent per stage, `crustify:<stage>`, and one assistant per campaign
  kind, `crustify:assistant-translate` and `crustify:assistant-audit`. A plugin agent's
  body replaces Claude Code's own system prompt, so each body opens with that prompt,
  `system-prompt.md`, followed by the generic provider's prompt without the skill index,
  since Claude Code lists the plugin's skills to every agent. Each agent's
  frontmatter gives the description the assistant routes a run by;
- `system-prompt.md`, Claude Code's own system prompt, captured from a real request by
  `dump-system-prompt.py`, less its one project's `# Memory` section, and dumped again
  when Claude Code is upgraded;
- `spawn.py`, which launches a stage run as a Claude Code process of its own, since Claude
  Code refuses a subagent's writes of report files, and copies its transcript into
  Crustify's home; the assistants' prompts end with how they launch through it;
- `hooks.json`: a `SubagentStop` hook, `transcripts.py`, which copies each stage agent's
  transcript into Crustify's home, for a stage run a host launches as a subagent; and
- `compose.py`, which generates the agents (`compose.py build`).

The generated files are committed, and regenerated whenever `agents/` or
`system-prompt.md` changes.

## 5. Language

Programmers and agents read Crustify's texts and a campaign's, so they are written plainly,
as the [Google developer documentation style guide](https://developers.google.com/style)
describes: one term per thing, short sentences, a condition before its consequence, lists for
parallel items. A rule keeps its reason, since agents generalize from reasons. A rewrite keeps
every fact of the old text, which its review checks. The voice rules of [Layers](#1-layers)
stay: a skill describes, an agent instructs.

description names, as `agents/common.md` says, and no other skill names a tool: the
description alone brings an agent to the tool, so it names every stage and step the tool
serves. A tool is removed by deleting its skill.

| text | goes in |
|---|---|
| what an artifact's fields mean | its schema skill under `skills/artifacts/` |
| what an artifact looks like | its example under `templates/` |
| how a kind of work is done, independent of tools | the skill for that work |
| how a kind of campaign proceeds, step by step | its workflow skill under `skills/workflows/`, with the steps every campaign shares in `setup` |
| a convention every agent follows | `conventions` |
| what one agent does, in which steps, and which steps it owns | that agent's file under `agents/` |
| what every agent holds | `agents/common.md` |
| what the assistant does in one kind of campaign | `agents/assistant/<kind>.md` |
| what a tool is, and how it serves each stage | its tool skill |
| how one host is served the layers | its provider under `providers/<host>/` |
| what one run needs beyond its role | its task message, `task.md` |
| what Crustify is for, which every change is judged against | `GOALS.md`, at Crustify's root |
| how Crustify repairs and improves itself | [`evolution`](../evolution/SKILL.md) |
| which changes landed, and whether each held | `EVOLUTION.md`, at Crustify's root |
| a rule that holds for one target alone | that campaign's `crustify/LESSONS.md` |

names a tool goes in the tool's skill. A change to a rule is made where the rule lives;
text that restates it elsewhere is removed rather than kept in step.

A stage's agent runs with its file as its system prompt and its task as its first message:
the task message names what its `## Inputs` section lists and the instructions its run
needs beyond its role, if any. Its file is the same for every run of the stage, so that runs at once share their

agent of a session in a campaign's repository, with its file and its campaign kind's as
its system prompt.

A provider serves the layers to one agent host, in that host's format, and holds nothing
the layers do not: every file it carries is generated from them, wires them in, or carries
what its host needs of its own.

`compose.py <agent> [<kind>]` prints `agents/common.md`, with the skill index filled, and
the agent's file, the assistant's with its campaign kind's. A host without a provider of
its own takes that prompt as its agent's instructions, and reads each skill's `SKILL.md`
by its path. The other providers compose through it.

The Claude Code provider, `providers/claude/`, makes Crustify's checkout a plugin, whose
manifest is `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`:

- the skills, by their group directories and the directory of each part of a split skill,
  which the manifest lists on its own since Claude Code scans a listed directory one level
  deep, invoked as `crustify:<name>`;
- `agents/`, one plugin agent per stage, `crustify:<stage>`, and one assistant per campaign
  kind, `crustify:assistant-translate` and `crustify:assistant-audit`. A plugin agent's
  body replaces Claude Code's own system prompt, so each body opens with that prompt,
  `system-prompt.md`, followed by the generic provider's prompt without the skill index,
  since Claude Code lists the plugin's skills to every agent. Each agent's
  frontmatter gives the description the assistant routes a run by;
- `system-prompt.md`, Claude Code's own system prompt, captured from a real request by
  `dump-system-prompt.py`, less its one project's `# Memory` section, and dumped again
  when Claude Code is upgraded;
- `spawn.py`, which launches a stage run as a Claude Code process of its own, since Claude
  Code refuses a subagent's writes of report files, and copies its transcript into
  Crustify's home; the assistants' prompts end with how they launch through it;
- `hooks.json`: a `SubagentStop` hook, `transcripts.py`, which copies each stage agent's
  transcript into Crustify's home, for a stage run a host launches as a subagent; and

`system-prompt.md` changes.

Programmers and agents read Crustify's texts and a campaign's, so they are written plainly,
as the [Google developer documentation style guide](https://developers.google.com/style)
describes: one term per thing, short sentences, a condition before its consequence, lists for
parallel items. A rule keeps its reason, since agents generalize from reasons. A rewrite keeps
every fact of the old text, which its review checks. The voice rules of [Layers](#1-layers)
stay: a skill describes, an agent instructs.

today, since a port turns the C that calls or supplies it into Rust, as
[`porting-symbols`](../../porting/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Function pointers section describes, and its safe API
does not change then. Its consumers see only the safe form, its closures taking and
returning safe types: a closure borrowed for the call, `impl FnMut(…)`, where C keeps it
for the call that receives it; an owned closure, released with its context, where C keeps
it until it releases it; and a trait, for a struct of function pointers a library calls
into, which Rust types and the C implementation implement alike. A function pointer read
from C, such as a field's getter returns, is the callable type, never the raw pointer.
How long C keeps it is a finding of the analysis.

Its trampoline is a panic barrier, which maps a panic to the C's error convention, and it
refuses a re-entrant call, which would alias an `FnMut` closure, unless the analysis shows
that C re-enters it, which takes an `Fn` closure instead. A function pointer C calls from
another thread takes a `Send` closure, and a `Sync` one when C may call it from several at
once. Four cases shape the type further:

- one without a context parameter carries no captured state: its Rust implementation is a
  closure without captures, each closure type its own trampoline, or a plain function;
- one C reads as absent when null, where it uses a default or calls nothing, is an
  `Option` of the callable type;
- one C compares with a known function, such as its default implementation, keeps in its C
  variant the pointer it was made from, so that the comparison still holds; and
- one whose context C reaches through another argument, such as the object it is handed,
  has a C half only for functions sound with any such argument. A C function that reads its
  context there is reached only through the object that holds it, by the routine that
  dispatches it with that object, and never as the callable type, whose safe call could
  hand it another object. A field or table that holds such functions is set from C, or
  through an `unsafe` setter whose contract carries the object's context, and is read back
  as no callable.

callback. The analysis establishes which of the object's routines C allows from within the
callback. One it does not allow, the function itself or one that resets the state the
function resumes from, is refused there by the binding, on the thread that runs the
function, since the callback holds an exclusive handle the borrow checker cannot tell from
any other.

named callable type over the one C function-pointer type.

# Item analysis

How a scheduled C item is analysed before it is bound or ported. The analysis is the same
for both: what it establishes shapes the binding or port that follows.

## 1. Scope

Each item is analysed from its source declarations and definitions, its dependency closure,
its callers, its field touchers and its existing Rust consumers. For every pointer field,
argument and return, every code path that stores, transfers, clones, retains or frees it is
inspected.

## 2. Findings

The analysis establishes:

- ownership and transfer direction;
- shared or mutable access;
- nullability;
- scalar, array, or other cardinality;
- type erasure and known element types;
- borrow and keepalive relationships;
- address retention: whether C keeps an object's address beyond the call that receives it,
  to read it, call back with it or free it;
- construction, clone, and destruction paths;
- states and transitions: the states each type's objects pass through, and the calls that
  move them between states, in the orders C allows, with the calls a callback may make on
  the object its caller lends it, and those that would corrupt the caller's state;
- out-parameters: the pointer arguments a function only writes through;
- string encodings, where a string is known to hold text or a path; and
- failure reporting: the status or sentinel returns and the error state beside the call
  through which a function fails, and the outcomes its callers treat as ordinary.

Observed behaviour overrides names and comments. A distinction the analysis establishes is
preserved in Rust rather than flattened into a copy of an ambiguous C signature.

name: soundness
description: "The patterns by which safe Rust over C has reached undefined behaviour in Crustify's campaigns, each with what prevents it and which check catches it, and how the catalogue grows from proven findings. Read before analysing, binding or porting any item, before writing its UB tests, and when reviewing for UB or contracts."
---

# Soundness patterns

The ways a binding or a port of C has let safe Rust reach undefined behaviour, or met a
memory-safety defect of the C that it had to keep out of its safe API. Every pattern here
has a proven finding of a campaign behind it: the catalogue records what went wrong, not
what could. An item's analysis asks of each pattern whether the item can meet it, and a
review for UB or contracts reads the item against the same list, so that a defect one
module met is not met again in the next.

## 1. Patterns

Each pattern has an id, which a finding's report names. What prevents a pattern is stated
as what the Rust does; [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md) and [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md)
give the routes that do it.

### 1.1 Values the C trusts

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unchecked-arithmetic` | The C computes with a value a safe caller controls and does not check it: a signed overflow, a shift, a size that wraps with its header, a zero divisor. | The Rust checks the value's range before the call, sizes past `isize::MAX` included, and refuses what the C would compute wrongly. | UBSan, review |
| `diverging-precheck` | A check in Rust repeats the C's parsing or evaluation and differs from what the C then computes. | The Rust validates the exact value the C will use, or computes the result itself and hands the C only that. | UBSan |
| `degenerate-input` | The C reads out of bounds on an input its own validation accepts, such as an empty string beside others or a null pointer for a string. | Every wrapper that can route the input to that reader refuses or normalises it, the indirect routes included. | ASan |
| `variant-mismatch` | A tagged, variable-size value of another variant than its container expects is passed on, and the C sizes its buffers by the container's. | The Rust compares the value's variant with the container's before any call that looks it up or formats it. | ASan |

### 1.2 Memory and ownership

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `size-known-to-c` | Only the C knows an object's true size or layout: an opaque type, a pointer a tag types, a base struct its callbacks read past, an array sized by a count. Rust builds it too small or types it wrongly. | Such an object is allocated through the C alone, a tagged pointer is typed only where its tag is vouched for, and an object whose callbacks read more than Rust built is refused. | ASan, review |
| `hidden-dependency` | A handle, a lent pointer or a callback outlives something it depends on without showing it: a parent it points back to, a global the program may close, lent memory the C copied into a second slot. | The handle's lifetime is tied to that owner, or it keeps the owner alive; a pointer the C stores is bounded by its longest-lived reader. | ASan, Miri, review |
| `failure-leaves-state` | A failure path of the C, most often a failed allocation, leaves an object uninitialised, freed, wrongly sized or half written and still returns, sometimes reporting success. | The Rust trusts nothing the C leaves after a failure: it validates outputs again, does not reuse the object, and composes the operation itself where the C's error path is unsafe. | ASan, UBSan, review |
| `allocator-rule` | The binding vouches for a rule of alignment or allocation that some build or allocator of the C does not keep: the maximum alignment, a zero-size resize, who may free whose storage. | It vouches only for what every configured allocator guarantees, and checks alignment at each constructor that copies. | Miri, UBSan, review |
| `adoption-condition` | An adoption takes ownership without stating when the C owns the storage: a sentinel pointer at zero capacity, one element listed twice, a buffer a pool still tracks. | The contract states the exact condition, and the Rust checks it before the owner can free or resize. | ASan, review |
| `count-wrap` | A reference count the C does not check wraps once safe Rust can leak clones, and the object is freed early. | A count that can wrap within a process's lifetime is checked before each increment, and the clone fails or aborts before it wraps. | Miri, review |
| `uninitialised-as-data` | Memory the C leaves unwritten is exposed as initialised Rust data, or the argument that the C writes it is false on some path. | The Rust views it as uninitialised until every path of the C is shown to write it; an export takes raw pointers and builds no reference over memory its caller may have left unwritten. | Miri, review |
| `aliasing-at-the-boundary` | A pointer the C keeps is derived from a borrow that a later reborrow ends, or Rust holds a reference over memory the C still writes or shares. | Every pointer the C keeps is derived from the original raw pointer, and a reference is handed out only over a span no C writer or co-owner reaches. | Miri, BSan, review |

### 1.3 Threads and callbacks

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unsynchronised-global` | The C reads and writes global state, or initialises it lazily on first use, without synchronisation, so that safe calls on unrelated objects race. | The Rust initialises or serialises that state before any safe call reaches it. | TSan, review |
| `assumed-locking` | A `Send` or `Sync` proof assumes the C object's own locking covers every access, but a path skips the lock, reads after releasing it, or the object has none. | Thread safety is derived from every reader and writer of each field. | review |
| `callback-state` | A trampoline mishandles a panic, a refusal or a re-entry: a stored panic goes stale or a nested call drops it, a drop panics, the C goes on after a refusal, or the callback runs under a lock of the C. | A stored panic or stop belongs to one outermost call of the C, no drop panics, and a stop is promised only where the C can be stopped. | review |

A `# Safety` contract or a `// SAFETY:` proof that is wrong in a way no pattern above names
is still a finding: a contract is derived again from every safe method that relies on it
whenever one is added.

## 2. Findings

A finding of the `ub` or `contracts` objective names its pattern, or `new`, as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s Reports section describes. A
sanitizer's false positive is no finding and names none.

A finding of a known pattern means that its statement did not let the analysis recognise
the case, or that what prevents it was not enough. A finding that is `new` is a pattern the
catalogue lacks.

## 3. Evolution

The catalogue changes only from findings a reproducer proves, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes:

- a `new` finding is proposed as a pattern once it is stated without the target's names,
  with the finding as its evidence; one that can only be stated in the target's names is
  that campaign's lesson;
- a pattern whose findings recur has its statement or its prevention sharpened, from the
  findings that escaped it; and
- a pattern no campaign has met since it was written stays: its absence is what the
  catalogue is for.

What tells whether the catalogue works is the count of findings of known patterns, over
the modules integrated since a pattern was written, taken together: it falls against the
modules before, or the catalogue is not what prevents them. One module alone tells nothing,
since modules differ. The unsafe sites the reviews read, which the count would be taken
against, are not recorded yet. The count of `new` findings tells how much of what goes wrong
the catalogue does not hold yet.

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |

whenever one is added.

A finding of the `ub` or `contracts` objective names its pattern, or `new`, as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s Reports section describes. A
sanitizer's false positive is no finding and names none.

the case, or that what prevents it was not enough. A finding that is `new` is a pattern the
catalogue lacks.

The catalogue changes only from findings a reproducer proves, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes:

- a pattern whose findings recur has its statement or its prevention sharpened, from the
  findings that escaped it; and
- a pattern no campaign has met since it was written stays: its absence is what the
  catalogue is for.

the modules integrated since a pattern was written, taken together: it falls against the
modules before, or the catalogue is not what prevents them. One module alone tells nothing,
since modules differ. The unsafe sites the reviews read, which the count would be taken
against, are not recorded yet. The count of `new` findings tells how much of what goes wrong
the catalogue does not hold yet.

- wrapped-layout projection;

They sit in their module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)'
Unsafe regions section lays them out, and a region's soundness rests on the region alone:
each item it exposes is sound for every input the rest of its module can give it, the
invariants its unsafe code relies on being held in the region's own private fields or
guaranteed by the library the bindings hold C memory through or the standard library, never by data the native code can build or
change. It exposes no field its unsafe code relies on, and no `unsafe fn` beyond the
public ones whose obligation no type expresses.

A confirmed C defect, a behaviour that departs from the C's specification as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s `logic` objective orders it, is not
carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the
binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it
composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the
C's order, correcting the defect, and its anchor is `Replaces`, as a port's is, its alias
kept. A lifecycle primitive that is defective only on a failure path is composed so,
while its policy still calls the primitives that are not. Each divergence is documented
on the item, and kept by a unit test, as [`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s
Equivalence tests section describes.

A dependency on a module that runs later, cut from a cycle, is reached through the safe
wrappers a wrap batch adds before its consumer, never through raw bindings. A wrapper over
the items of a module that will be ported is written as that module's API: the names,
ownership and error types its port keeps, so that its consumers do not change when it
ports. Every unsafe block carries
the safety comment [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section specifies.

An out-of-tree library's entity, such as libc's or libm's, is reached through the Rust
standard library wherever it provides it and the state the entity works on stays in Rust,
or crosses to C only as values the boundary converts: `errno` set from an `io::Error` by
an export gateway, a `struct stat` filled from an `fs::Metadata`. It is reached through the
library's bindings wherever that state is shared with C: a lock, a handle or an allocation
the remaining C uses too. `dependencies.json` recommends a route for each entity, which a
library's `decision` adopts or overrides; the first batch that needs the entity checks that
route against the code it translates, takes another the decision allows where it does not
hold, and reports which in its final message, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Confirmation section describes. An
entity needed through a wrapper that lacks it is reported, never reached through raw
bindings.

# ffibox

ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions
through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held
from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its
primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a
value; what C does not alias is plain Rust.

Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which
primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A
representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md`
describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals,
`docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there.

## Planning

### Dependencies › Adopted crates

A candidate crate's soundness is read against the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists,
each of which ffibox excludes from the campaign's own bindings: the crate qualifies where
its safe API excludes them too, by whatever means it uses.

## Binding workflow

### Binding workflow › Rust tree

The workspace depends on ffibox by path, on the checkout the host provides, which is on
the campaign's working branch of it, `ffibox = { path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox" }` in Crustify's image, so that
each run records its revision among its task's `revisions`. The path is the checkout's
canonical one, with no symbolic link on it, and a `[patch]` that redirects another source of
ffibox names the same: compile-fail snapshots normalize a path dependency only where the
compiler's paths match the dependency's canonical directory.

Until then the path leaves the crate, against `bindgen`'s Layout section, and pins no
revision. -->

## Binding and porting

Binding reads `docs/ownership.md`, `docs/borrows.md`, `docs/patterns.md`,
`docs/vtables.md` and `docs/hand-written.md`; porting reads `docs/outbound.md` too.

### Binding types

A type that stays interoperable with C is bound through ffibox's primitives wherever they
apply, as `docs/ownership.md` and `docs/borrows.md` walk from its C declaration to them.

### Binding types › Safe layout

While a type keeps its C layout, `define_ctype!` mints `Foo`, `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`,
and its owners are aliases of ffibox's owners over the policy that names its lifecycle
routines: `pub type FooBox = CBox<Foo, FooFree>;`, and `CArc<Foo, P>` for `FooArc`. A
value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal<Foo, P>`.

### Binding symbols › Functions

A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned

iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them.

`CTable` whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints, over the binding's own `unsafe impl CVtable`, as

only `'static`, its caller stating the threads C uses. Where the binding has one owner for every table of that type, C's and Rust's alike (`CBox`, whose policy calls the `free` slot), the surrendered pointer is adopted into it with `from_c`, `unsafe` as every adoption is: its obligation is that the policy releases through the `free` slot. ffibox does not add a trait for that obligation, which is one block per table type. ### (c) Receivers and re-entry A slot declares its receiver in its body's argument type: `|s: &S|` is a **shared** slot, `|s: &mut S|` an **exclusive** one, inferred by `enter` from the closure, so a slot cannot get a receiver it did not declare. The entry state is a non-blocking read-write lock over `S`, as `RwLock::try_read` / `try_write` are: - any number of shared slots run at once, re-entrant or on several threads; - an exclusive slot runs only when no other slot does; - a slot that cannot enter, an exclusive one while another slot runs or a shared one while an exclusive one does, is **refused**: it returns the value it declares `on busy`, without reaching `S`. So re-entry is declared per slot, by its receiver, and a table whose slots all take `&S` is never refused. The owner's own accessors take part: `state(&self)` lends `&S` and refuses exclusive slots until the owner is next borrowed mutably (it cannot see when the `&S` ends, so it waits for the `&mut self` that proves it has); `state_mut` and `as_mut` take `&mut self`. Release follows the same state. C's `free` while a slot runs, re-entrantly from inside it or on another thread, is deferred: the slot that exits last frees the allocation, on its own thread, and every slot entered while the drop is deferred is refused. A `free` C calls on a table the owner still holds is deferred to the owner's drop, and forgotten if the owner then surrenders the table to C, which holds it anew. Each allocation is dropped exactly once, whichever order C and Rust release it in. ### (d) Panics ==== - **C frees it.** The memory comes from the allocator C frees with. If that is C's own (`free`, `lib_free`), build it through that allocator's policy: `CVec::from_fn` and `CVec::new_uninit` with a `CLenAlloc` policy, `CVec::from_slice` and `CStrBox::from_c_str` with a copying one, or a `Box` / `Vec` over `CAllocator

Then surrender it with `into_raw`. - **C calls back during the call** (`foreach`, `qsort_r`). `CClosure::new` over `&mut F`. The trampoline's type is inferred from the C declaration it is passed to, and the closure's arguments are the C types, which the binding converts to handles before calling its consumer's closure. With `std`, a panic stops the C routine through the failure value and resumes after it, at `finish()`; a re-entrant invocation is refused the same way. `F: Send` unless the routine calls back on the calling thread only (`unsafe CClosure::new_local`). - **C keeps the callback** (`set_log_callback(cb, ctx, free)`). `CPayload` over an `Fn` closure, surrendered with `into_raw`, released by C through `release_fn()`. C may call it from several threads or re-entrantly, so it is reached as `&F`, and `into_raw` requires `Send + Sync`; state it changes goes behind a `Mutex` or an atomic. A panic in it aborts, so a fallible body goes in `barrier`. - **C keeps a value** (a container's payload, user data). `CPayload`, and `CPayload::borrow` inside the callbacks that receive it. - **C hands Rust a callback** (an options struct's `progress_cb` and `payload`, a ported function's `cb, ctx` arguments through its export). `CFn::new`, `unsafe`, states what the C that supplies the pair guarantees; `call((args…))` takes C's argument types, the context left out, so the binding's safe callable converts its arguments and calls in one justified block. `parts()` hands the pair to another C routine unchanged, with no trampoline between. - **A callable is either** (a field a consumer sets with a closure and C sets with a function, a callback ported code calls whoever supplied it). `CCallback` / `CCallbackBox` hold whichever it is: called from Rust, a closure runs through its trampoline, with the same refusal and panic handling as when C calls it, and handed to C, a C function goes as its own pair. - **C calls into a table Rust implements** (`git_config_backend`, a `git_writestream`: a struct of function pointers, each passed the table). `CTable`, the state `S` behind the table of the layout type `T`, whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints from the trait `S` implements: each slot declares its receiver, `&S` or `&mut S`, which decides what re-entry it allows, and its results for a panic and a refusal. **Verdict: rejected, with one required fix, which only removes text.** The rule itself is sound and well placed. What is wrong is the record row the proposal drafts: as written, it would miss the signal coming back.

I read crustify `6ad1ea5` under `libgit2-crustify/devel` (`e8e55af`). I changed nothing, committed nothing and filed nothing. Per your instruction, I ran no gate and no rerun. My only scratch is `crustify/tmp/review-callback-reenters/`, which I used to confirm the change applies on `e8e55af` without `15845fd`. It does, so the two changes are independent.

## Required fix

**The row's recurrence signal is limited to the `callback-state` pattern, and this case is not one.** In the `soundness` skill, `callback-state` covers "a trampoline mishandles a panic, a refusal or a re-entry". Here the trampoline handles nothing wrongly: the binding of the caller's own routine is what fails to refuse the call. A reviewer reading the catalogue (§2) would file a recurrence as `new`, and possibly under `contracts` rather than `ub`. Either way it would not match the row, so the row would never be marked `recurred`.
- **Fix by removal:** delete "of the `callback-state` pattern", and change "a `ub` finding" to "a finding".

## Checks that pass

- **Evidence and signal:** the evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it. The cited UB tests exist (`tests/ub_unsafe/deps/llhttp/llhttp.rs:639`, `:664`), and so does a test that a handler may still parse a different parser. The handlers are capture-free callable types, which confirms the gap: the existing re-entry rule only protects closure state.
- **Goal and placement:** it serves Safety. It sits where `authoring` puts it, uses no target names, and needs no ffibox primitive.
- **Consistency:** it does not contradict the trampoline's re-entry rule or `15845fd`'s fourth case. It agrees with ffibox's `outbound.md` (a `CClosure` refuses re-entry) and with `vtables.md` §(c) (a per-object entry state).
- **Soundness catalogue:** adding no pattern is consistent with the skill's §3, because no review finding has proven this case yet.
- **Checks and protected paths:** it weakens no check and touches no protected path, so it can land once approved without the user's sign-off.
- **Validation:** none was run. The proposal argues a rerun would reproduce the same binding, and I accept that, as you instructed.

## Not required (they do not affect the verdict)

1. **The examples read as the whole list.** "One it does not allow, the function itself or one that resets…" reads as closed. "Such as" would fix that. Also, "resets" is narrower than `analysis`' "corrupt the caller's state".
2. **"On the thread that runs the function" is one implementation, not the rule.** It describes the batch's thread-local register. It misses a callback C runs on another thread, while ffibox's per-object entry state covers that case. The clause can simply be removed.
3. **The stated reason assumes one kind of handle.** "The borrow checker cannot tell [the handle] from any other" holds only when the callback gets the general exclusive handle. A binding could instead give the callback a handle type that lacks the disallowed routines, refusing them at compile time. The reason also does not cover a shared handle.
4. **The proposal cites a signal §2 does not list.** "A rule … a binding had to work out by hand" is not a row of `evolution` §2's table. The real grounds are one batch, the user's direction after triage, and a gap in the spec that left UB reachable. Separately, `agents/common.md` names "a rule you had to work out by hand" as evidence, but §2 has no matching row. That gap belongs to the evolution guidance, and I am only reporting it here, not filing it.
5. **The recurrence signal could be narrower.** "Calls a routine of the object" could say "a routine C does not allow there".
6. **Testing has no matching item yet.** The `testing` skill's UB-test list (`skills/verification/testing/SKILL.md:96`) says "reenter a callback" but not "re-enter the caller through the lent object". It is a protected path, so a change there would be a proposal of its own.
